articles.excerpt: Dr Kunal Sood explains the science behind a bedtime habit gaining traction on social media — and why stable blood sugar may be the key to staying asleep through the night.
articles.image_caption: A jar of peanut butter, which US physician Dr Kunal Sood recommends as a bedtime snack for better sleep. The spread contains tryptophan, magnesium and healthy fats that may help stabilise overnight blood sugar levels.
articles.nri_angle: The tip from Indian-origin physician Dr Kunal Sood resonates with health-conscious South Asian professionals managing hectic schedules and late-night routines abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: How to Pick the Perfect Breathable Kurta for Summer's Worst Heat
articles.excerpt: From cotton and mulmul to linen and chanderi, a practical guide to staying cool and stylish when the mercury climbs.
articles.image_caption: A woman wears an Ajrakh-printed cotton kurta, one of many breathable ethnic wear options suited for extreme summer heat. Lightweight fabrics like cotton, mulmul, and linen are increasingly popular choices for warm-weather dressing.
articles.nri_angle: Guide helps diaspora members choose comfortable ethnic wear for summer visits to India or for warm-weather styling abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ultra-Processed Foods in Childhood Linked to Insulin Resistance and Prediabetes Risk
articles.excerpt: A growing body of research shows that diets heavy in packaged snacks, sugary drinks, and fast food during childhood and young adulthood can disrupt blood sugar regulation and increase the risk of type 2 diabetes, with implications for Indian diaspora families navigating food environments in the West.
articles.image_caption: Ultra-processed foods have been linked to rising childhood insulin resistance, according to a new systematic review
articles.nri_angle: South Asian children in the diaspora face compounded risk: genetic predisposition to insulin resistance at lower body weights combined with Western food environments dominated by ultra-processed products.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Updated U.S. Heart Guidelines Expand Statin Eligibility to Adults as Young as 30
articles.excerpt: The 2026 ACC/AHA guidelines lower risk thresholds and adopt a new calculator that could reshape cholesterol management for millions of Americans, with particular implications for South Asian communities at elevated cardiovascular risk.
articles.image_caption: Updated guidelines recommend statin therapy for adults as young as 30 with elevated cardiovascular risk factors
articles.nri_angle: South Asian ancestry is explicitly listed as a risk-enhancing factor in the 2026 ACC/AHA guidelines, which could prompt earlier cholesterol screening and statin conversations for Indian diaspora communities.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: HIIT Workouts Can Reverse Cellular Aging by Nearly a Decade, Studies Show
articles.excerpt: Multiple peer-reviewed studies find that high-intensity interval training boosts mitochondrial function, lengthens telomeres, and rolls back biological age markers in adults over 65.
articles.image_caption: Studies show HIIT workouts can reverse cellular aging by nearly a decade
articles.nri_angle: The findings are particularly relevant for India's urban population and its diaspora, where rising rates of diabetes and cardiovascular disease make time-efficient, high-impact exercise protocols increasingly important.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: FDA Panel to Decide Fate of America's Booming Peptide Market This Week
articles.excerpt: As the FDA's advisory committee meets July 23-24 to debate whether seven popular peptides can be legally compounded in the U.S., telehealth startups and wellness clinics are already positioning to cash in — while safety experts warn the science simply isn't there yet.
articles.image_caption: The FDA's advisory panel is set to review the future of compounded peptide therapies
articles.nri_angle: Indian Americans constitute roughly 10% of U.S. physicians and face growing patient inquiries about unapproved peptides. If the FDA loosens restrictions, Indian pharmaceutical companies already dominant in generic drug manufacturing could find new compounding market opportunities.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Jensen Huang's $75 Million Gift to Vanderbilt Puts Art and Design at Heart of San Francisco Campus
articles.excerpt: The Nvidia CEO and his wife's landmark matching donation will establish a new college of art, architecture and design on the site of the closing California College of the Arts.
articles.image_caption: Jensen Huang, co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, whose $75 million matching gift will establish a new college of art, architecture and design at Vanderbilt University's San Francisco campus.
articles.nri_angle: The new college at the nexus of art, design, and technology in San Francisco is relevant to the large Indian diaspora in Bay Area tech, and the Huang philanthropy model offers a framework for investing in arts alongside STEM.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: CVS Pharmacies Nationwide Now Fill Prescriptions for Dogs and Cats
articles.excerpt: The pharmacy giant has expanded into pet healthcare, allowing owners to fill veterinary prescriptions at approximately 9,000 locations across the United States — with delivery, automatic refills, and app management included.
articles.image_caption: CVS pharmacies across the U.S. now fill veterinary prescriptions for pets
articles.nri_angle: CVS's pet pharmacy expansion is relevant for Indian American pet owners, a growing demographic that increasingly treats pets as family. The convenience of filling pet prescriptions at the same pharmacy used for family medications, with app-based management and delivery, appeals to busy diaspora households.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Spouses of Dementia Patients Face Up to Sixfold Higher Risk of Developing the Disease
articles.excerpt: Multiple studies across the US, South Korea and Norway point to shared lifestyles, caregiving stress and modifiable risk factors as drivers of elevated dementia risk within married couples.
articles.image_caption: An elderly couple sits together at home. Research shows that when one spouse develops dementia, the other faces a significantly elevated risk of the same condition due to shared lifestyles and caregiving stress.
articles.nri_angle: The findings are relevant to Indian diaspora families where multigenerational caregiving is culturally expected, and where spousal caregivers may face compounded stress from managing health responsibilities alongside immigration and settlement challenges.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: WHO Says 45% of Dementia Cases Are Preventable, Adds Air Pollution and Hearing Aids to Guidelines
articles.excerpt: The World Health Organization's first major dementia prevention update since 2019 introduces air pollution as a new risk factor and recommends hearing aids to reduce cognitive decline, while warning against certain popular supplements.
articles.image_caption: An audiologist examines a patient's hearing with an otoscope during a clinical assessment. The WHO now recommends hearing aids as a strategy to reduce dementia risk, upgrading its 2019 guidance that called only for screening.
articles.nri_angle: India has a higher proportion of modifiable dementia risk factors than high-income countries, with 41% hearing loss prevalence and widespread air pollution from solid fuel cooking affecting both residents and the families of diaspora Indians.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Inhaling CO2 Cleared Alzheimer's Proteins in Early Human Trial
articles.excerpt: A 30-minute session of intermittent high-dose carbon dioxide inhalation flushed toxic proteins from the brain by mimicking deep-sleep cleansing mechanisms, while a separate copper-based drug showed similar promise in mice.
articles.image_caption: An MRI brain scan displayed on a computer screen in a clinical setting. Researchers presented new findings on clearing Alzheimer's-linked proteins at the Alzheimer's Association International Conference in London.
articles.nri_angle: India has an estimated 8.8 million people living with dementia, and the findings on accessible treatments like CO2 inhalation could prove especially relevant for diaspora families managing elder care across borders.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Women With PCOS Face Four Times Higher Risk of Heart Disease, Lancet Study Finds
articles.excerpt: A major US study of more than 413,000 women found those with the recently renamed condition had a fourfold increase in cardiovascular disease risk, even after accounting for obesity and diabetes.
articles.image_caption: A doctor measures a patient's blood pressure during a clinical consultation. A new Lancet study has found women with PCOS, now renamed PMOS, face four times the risk of heart disease.
articles.nri_angle: PCOS prevalence in India ranges from 7% to 20%, and South Asian women face elevated baseline cardiovascular risk, making the study's findings of compounding heart disease risk especially relevant for the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Fully Human Antibody Halts Aggressive Prostate Cancer Spread in Preclinical Study
articles.excerpt: Researchers at Sweden's Umeå University developed a drug made entirely from human proteins that stopped both tumor growth and metastasis through a novel mechanism, raising hopes for men with advanced disease.
articles.image_caption: A researcher works with samples in a laboratory setting. The new antibody drug was developed at Umeå University in Sweden and targets a novel biological pathway in aggressive prostate cancer.
articles.nri_angle: Prostate cancer rates are rising among Indian men and the diaspora, making new treatment breakthroughs directly relevant to community health.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Indian Doctors Validate CRIB-II Score as Key Predictor of Mortality in Premature Newborns
articles.excerpt: A growing body of research from Indian hospitals confirms that the CRIB-II scoring system outperforms other tools in identifying premature neonates at highest risk of in-hospital death, with accuracy rates exceeding 88 percent.
articles.image_caption: A medical professional caring for a newborn in a hospital setting. Recent Indian studies have validated the CRIB-II scoring system as a reliable predictor of mortality risk in premature neonates admitted to NICUs.
articles.nri_angle: Indian-origin physicians and diaspora-led medical NGOs can use CRIB-II validation data to guide neonatal care investments and training programs in India.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Your Thymus May Decide How Long You Live, Two Major Studies Find
articles.excerpt: Harvard-led research published in Nature reveals the long-overlooked chest gland strongly predicts longevity, cardiovascular risk, and cancer immunotherapy outcomes in adults.
articles.image_caption: A CT scanner of the kind used in the Harvard-led studies that analyzed thymic health in more than 27,000 adults. The research linked thymus condition to longevity and cancer immunotherapy outcomes.
articles.nri_angle: Immunotherapy use is expanding rapidly across India's cancer centres and among diaspora patients; thymic health scores could eventually help clinicians personalise treatment for Indian-origin patients worldwide.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Last Iron Lung Users Are Gone, but Polio Still Isn't
articles.excerpt: With the deaths of Paul Alexander and Martha Lillard, the iron lung era has ended in the United States — yet experts warn that the virus remains a global threat, particularly as vaccine hesitancy grows.
articles.image_caption: Paul Alexander in his iron lung in 1986. He contracted polio at age six in 1952 and spent the next 72 years in the device, becoming the Guinness World Record holder for longest time in an iron lung.
articles.nri_angle: India eliminated polio in 2014 through a massive vaccination campaign — a public health triumph the diaspora can take pride in. But with wild poliovirus still circulating in neighboring Pakistan and vaccine hesitancy growing globally, the story remains unfinished.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Heart Attacks in Your 20s and 30s: Why India's Young Are Dying of a Disease Their Grandparents Survived
articles.excerpt: Cardiologists warn that half of all heart attacks in Indian men now occur before the age of 50, driven by a toxic combination of sedentary lifestyles, chronic stress, and genetic predisposition.
articles.image_caption: A young man getting a health checkup. Cardiologists warn that heart attacks among Indians aged 20-30 are rising 2% annually.
articles.nri_angle: South Asian immigrants in the US and UK face 2-4x higher coronary disease rates than the general population. Cardiologists recommend screening by age 30 for Indians abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: America's GLP-1 Drug Use Surges as Semaglutide Dominates and Costs Climb
articles.excerpt: A new study finds GLP-1 receptor agonist use grew by 230% among diabetics and 643% among non-diabetics between 2017 and 2022, with semaglutide driving the boom — but total per-person spending is rising even as out-of-pocket costs fall.
articles.image_caption: YouTube / Minute USA
articles.image_credit: Photo by Markus Winkler on Pexels

sources.label: Journal of the American Heart Association
Journal of Managed Care and Specialty Pharmacy

articles.nri_angle: South Asians face elevated risks of Type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease at lower BMIs, making GLP-1 drug access and affordability especially relevant for the Indian American community.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Minoxidil: The Go-To Solution for Hair Growth
articles.excerpt: Exploring the surge in popularity of minoxidil among those facing hair loss.
articles.image_caption: minoxidil
articles.nri_angle: Minoxidil offers NRIs an effective solution for hair loss, addressing cultural beauty standards.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Drinking Up to Five Cups of Coffee a Day May Lower Stroke and Diabetes Risk, Major Study Finds
articles.excerpt: An umbrella review of over 100 meta-analyses finds consistent evidence that moderate coffee consumption is associated with reduced risk of several chronic diseases, though experts caution results vary by preparation method.
articles.image_caption: A cup of freshly brewed coffee. A comprehensive review of over 100 meta-analyses found that moderate coffee consumption is linked to reduced risk of stroke, type 2 diabetes and several other chronic conditions.
articles.nri_angle: India is one of the world's largest coffee-producing nations, and filter coffee is integral to South Indian culture; the findings are relevant to diaspora communities who maintain these traditions.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Filtered Coffee Linked to Slower Biological Aging While Instant Coffee Shows Opposite Effect
articles.excerpt: A UK Biobank study of nearly 50,000 people found divergent associations between coffee brewing types and biological aging markers, with inflammation as a possible mediating pathway
articles.image_caption: A pour-over coffee setup with a glass carafe and paper filter. A new study found that filtered coffee was associated with slower biological aging compared to instant coffee.
articles.nri_angle: For South Indian diaspora households where filter coffee is a daily ritual, the study offers modest reassurance about their preferred brewing method.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: PCOS Renamed PMOS as Landmark Study Links Condition to Four-Fold Higher Heart Disease Risk
articles.excerpt: A new Lancet study shows women with the condition formerly known as PCOS face quadruple the risk of cardiovascular disease, adding urgency to a global push for better screening and earlier intervention.
articles.image_caption: A woman undergoes a health screening at a medical facility. New research links PMOS, the condition formerly known as PCOS, to a four-fold increase in cardiovascular disease risk.
articles.nri_angle: One in five Indian women is affected by PMOS, making this renaming and the new heart disease data directly relevant to millions in the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: People With Type 2 Diabetes Face Up to 25 Times Higher Risk of Severe Dengue, Review Warns
articles.excerpt: A comprehensive review highlights that diabetic patients who contract dengue for the first time face dramatically worse outcomes, a finding with urgent relevance as India enters peak monsoon season.
articles.image_caption: A close-up of a mosquito feeding on human skin in Bilaspur, India. Research shows people with type 2 diabetes who contract dengue for the first time face dramatically higher odds of developing severe disease.
articles.nri_angle: India has the world's second-largest diabetes population and sees hundreds of thousands of dengue cases annually, making this finding critical for NRIs visiting family during monsoon season.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A 10-Minute Walk After Meals Can Slash Blood Sugar Spikes, and Experts Say Indians Need It Most
articles.excerpt: Multiple studies show a short post-meal walk lowers glucose levels more effectively than a single long workout, a habit that could help the millions of Indians at risk of Type 2 diabetes.
articles.image_caption: A person walks along a path after a meal. Research shows that even a leisurely 10-minute stroll within 30 minutes of eating can significantly reduce post-meal blood sugar spikes.
articles.nri_angle: Indians are genetically predisposed to Type 2 diabetes and develop it a decade earlier, making post-meal walking habits especially relevant.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Night Owls Carry More Belly Fat and Higher Blood Sugar, Major Study Finds
articles.excerpt: A study of nearly 300 women published in Frontiers in Nutrition links evening chronotype to poorer metabolic health, higher body fat percentages, and less nutritious food choices — even when total calorie intake is similar.
articles.image_caption: A woman works on her laptop late at night. New research links being a night owl to higher body fat, elevated blood sugar, and poorer metabolic health markers.
articles.nri_angle: The findings are relevant for the Indian diaspora, where long working hours and late-night eating patterns are common, and where diabetes and metabolic syndrome rates are already elevated.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Fatty Pancreas Now Recognised as a Disease, Linked to Diabetes and Cancer Risk
articles.excerpt: An international panel of experts has formally classified fatty pancreas as a distinct disease entity, establishing a clinical framework that connects pancreatic fat accumulation to type 2 diabetes and pancreatic cancer.
articles.image_caption: An anatomical illustration of the human pancreas and surrounding organs. International experts have formally classified fat accumulation in the pancreas as a distinct disease linked to diabetes and cancer.
articles.nri_angle: The classification has significant implications for Indians, who face among the world's highest rates of type 2 diabetes and are increasingly affected by metabolic syndrome at younger ages.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: AI Can Spot Pancreatic Cancer Up to 16 Months Before Doctors, Johns Hopkins Surgeon Says
articles.excerpt: A Johns Hopkins researcher highlights advances in AI-powered cancer detection that could transform outcomes for one of the deadliest cancers, while a new vaccine shows promise in intercepting the disease.
articles.image_caption: A medical professional reviews diagnostic imaging on a screen. Johns Hopkins researchers are developing AI tools that could detect pancreatic cancer up to 16 months earlier than human readers.
articles.nri_angle: Pancreatic cancer disproportionately affects South Asians; AI-driven early detection breakthroughs at institutions like Johns Hopkins could improve outcomes for the Indian diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Excessive TV Watching in Midlife Linked to Brain Shrinkage and Memory Loss, New Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Researchers found that frequent television viewers in their 40s and 50s showed smaller brain volumes and greater white matter damage decades later — and exercise alone may not offset the risk.
articles.image_caption: A medical professional examines a brain scan on a monitor. New research links excessive midlife TV watching to reduced brain volume in areas associated with memory.
articles.nri_angle: Evening TV watching is deeply embedded in Indian family routines; findings suggest simple lifestyle adjustments could protect brain health.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: India Gets Its First Multi-Cancer Blood Test as Dr Dangs Lab Partners With Zydus and Guardant Health
articles.excerpt: The Shield test can screen for 10 common cancers from a single blood draw, marking a significant step toward early detection in a country where most cancers are diagnosed at advanced stages.
articles.image_caption: A laboratory technician processes blood samples for diagnostic testing. Dr Dangs Lab has become the first laboratory in India to offer Guardant Health's multi-cancer detection blood test nationwide.
articles.nri_angle: NRIs with family in India can now access advanced multi-cancer screening through a simple blood test, potentially enabling early detection for parents and relatives back home.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
